verified_claims: The lexicographic measure (K, S) where K = count of integers > 1 and S = sum of Ω(x) strictly decreases with every legal move, guaranteeing termination.
At termination exactly one integer M > 1 remains because the total product never exceeds the initial product (> 1) and cannot exceed 1 if all numbers were 1.
For each prime p, the gcd of the multiset of p-adic valuations is invariant under the operation (a,b) → (min(a,b), |a-b|).
At termination, the final integer M has p-adic valuation equal to this invariant gcd, so M = ∏_p p^{gcd_i v_p(a_i)}.
The final integer M is independent of the sequence of moves chosen.
summary: The proof is complete, correct, and rigorous. Part 1 uses a well-founded lexicographic measure (K, sum Ω) to prove termination with exactly one integer M > 1. Part 2 establishes the invariant that for each prime p, the gcd of the multiset of p-adic valuations is preserved (since (a,b) → (min(a,b), |a-b|) preserves the multiset gcd, being a Euclidean algorithm step). Termination from Part 1 guarantees exactly one integer M > 1 at termination, so for each prime p the multiset of p-adic valuations is {v_p(M), 0, ..., 0} whose gcd is v_p(M). By invariance, v_p(M) equals the initial gcd of p-adic exponents, giving M = ∏ p^{gcd_i v_p(a_i)} uniquely determined by the initial multiset. All claims are verified; no fatal gaps or missing steps. The proof is self-contained, uses only elementary number theory and well-foundedness of ℕ², and correctly identifies that 2026 is arbitrary (works for any N ≥ 2).
transfer_assessment: Lexicographic descent with well-founded measure is a transferable termination technique for combinatorial processes.
The prime-exponent gcd invariant is a powerful transferable technique: gcd of a multiset is invariant under pairwise Euclidean steps, useful for many invariant problems.
The endgame analysis—using termination to force a canonical final configuration that reveals the invariant—is a transferable proof pattern for confluence/uniqueness problems.
The distinction between gcd of exponents vs min of exponents (exponent-wise gcd vs integer gcd) is a transferable number-theory insight.
The proof structure (termination + invariant + endgame) is a reusable template for IMO-style process problems.
